keyword: how to become a UI/UX designer after 10th
title: How to Become a UI/UX Designer After 10th (2026)
desc: How to become a UI/UX designer after Class 10: user research, wireframes, visual design and prototypes, with a yearly plan, projects and salary.
h1: How to become a UI/UX designer after 10th
research, screens and a real portfolio
lead: A plan for a Class 10 student and their parent to read together. It follows a real 624-hour, three-year design curriculum, where the whole first year is about UI and UX: research, layout, wireframes and prototypes.
role_intro: A UI/UX designer makes apps and websites easy and pleasant to use. The UX part means talking to users, finding where they get stuck and planning the flow. The UI part means the screens: layout, type, colour, buttons and how they respond when tapped.
in_short: Yes, you can start after Class 10. No drawing talent or design background is assumed. Careful observation matters more.
Year 1 is fully about UI and UX: visual design, user research, information architecture, wireframes, interaction design and prototypes.
Your portfolio is your real qualification. Design employers look at case studies first, so every month ends with a piece of work you can show.
start_answer: Yes. You can start learning UI/UX design right after Class 10, because the program assumes no design background and begins with visual basics and how real people use the apps on their phones.
start_bridge: UI/UX design is open to every stream, which is unusual in tech. The stream mostly changes which degree you take alongside it.
streams: Design, psychology, communication and fine arts degrees. Psychology in particular helps with user research.
B.Tech through JEE Main needs Physics and Mathematics, so engineering routes close.
B.Tech, BCA or B.Sc, which suits designers who also want to understand code.
A heavy entrance load can squeeze design practice. Keep a small weekly habit going.
BBA and business degrees, which help later with product and business decisions.
Some design colleges run their own entrance tests. Check each college's rules early.
start_extra: Many UI/UX designers in India did not study design in school. What matters is a portfolio that shows how you think. Show the problem, the research, the options you tried and why you chose the final screen.
roadmap_answer: The roadmap gives year 1 to core UI and UX skills, year 2 to product thinking and design systems, and year 3 to advanced research, accessibility, AI interfaces and a professional portfolio.
year_focus: Year 1: learn to see, research and design clear screens
Year 2: design whole products and reusable design systems
Year 3: design for everyone, including AI features, and build your portfolio
fit_note: The program's published tools list names only GitHub, so this page does not promise training in any particular design software. Ask on enquiry which tools the classes use. The program also does not teach drawing, illustration or animation as separate skills.
skills_answer: A UI/UX designer needs visual design, user research, information architecture, wireframing, interaction design, UI layout, prototyping, accessibility and the habit of testing designs with real users before calling them finished.
skills: Spacing, type and colour decide whether a screen feels clear or messy.
Talking to and watching users shows what they really need.
Organises menus and content so people find things fast.
Plans a screen's structure before any colour or detail.
What happens when a user taps, swipes or makes a mistake.
Turns wireframes into finished, consistent screens.
A clickable version you can test before anything is built.
Checks a design against known principles and real users.
Makes screens work for people with low vision or other needs.
build_answer: You finish one design project every month, so year 1 alone gives you twelve pieces, from recreated app screens to a complete UX case study, and three years give you 36.
projects: Copying good screens trains your eye for spacing and layout.
UX audit of a real product
Finding real problems in an app you already use.
Your first interviews and observations with real people.
The plan of an app before any visual polish.
A clickable flow you can put in front of users.
A set of consistent buttons, forms and cards for a website.
Your first full portfolio piece, from research to final screens.
Proof that you design for everyone, including AI features.
certs_answer: UI/UX certificates from Google, CalArts and IxDF can show an employer that you studied the basics properly, but each is awarded by its own provider, and design hiring still depends mostly on your portfolio.

cert_notes.Google UX Design Professional Certificat: A beginner-level series on Coursera covering UX research, information architecture, wireframing, prototyping, usability testing and responsive web design. Google says no degree or experience is required.
cert_notes.CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization: A 4-course series on Coursera from the California Institute of the Arts. It covers visual elements of UI design, UX fundamentals, information architecture and prototypes.
cert_notes.IxDF UX Certification: IxDF courses are self-paced, with a certificate for each course you finish. IxDF says grading is done by experts, and its course list includes "User Experience: The Beginner's Guide".

cert_extra: These three sit in year 1, in the UX Foundations, UI Design and Year-1 Capstone modules. The NN/g UX Certification comes later, in year 3.
notfor_answer: This path is not for you if you want to make art for its own sake, dislike feedback on your work, or prefer working alone, because UI/UX design means designing for other people and changing your ideas when users struggle.
notfor: You want to make art for yourself.
UI/UX is about what users need, not personal style. Illustration or fine arts may suit you better.
Criticism of your work upsets you.
Designs are reviewed and tested all the time. Changing them is normal.
You would rather not talk to strangers.
User research means interviewing and watching real people.
No honest course can promise a job, salary or exam pass, and this one does not.
You need a degree and nothing else.
This program awards a NeuroNetworks AI Ed certificate, not a degree. Many students take it alongside school and college.
salary_answer: Indicative ranges for product and UX roles in India are about ₹4 to 8 lakh a year for freshers, ₹10 to 22 lakh at 3 to 5 years, and ₹25 to 50 lakh or more at senior level.
faqs: How many years does it take to become a UI/UX designer after 10th?

Core UI and UX skills take about a year in this roadmap. The full 3-year, 624-hour Product & UX / AI Design program builds a professional portfolio. Some employers also ask for a degree, so many students study it alongside Class 11, 12 and college.
Can I become a UI/UX designer without maths?

Yes. UI/UX design needs observation, empathy and clear thinking more than advanced maths. Mathematics matters only if you also want a B.Tech through JEE Main, which needs Physics and Mathematics in Class 12.
Do I need to be good at drawing to become a UI/UX designer?
No. Most UI work is layout, spacing and type, not drawing. The program starts with visual design fundamentals and assumes no design background.
What is the difference between UI and UX design?
UX design is how a product works for its users: the research, the flow and the problems it solves. UI design is how the screens look and respond. Most junior roles in India ask for both.
Does the program include AI in UI/UX design?
Yes, from year 2. Students study AI UX patterns and AI prototyping, then build an accessible AI interface and AI design systems in year 3.
context_fact: Nasscom's Strategic Review 2026 describes AI moving from optional to core infrastructure in India's tech industry. As more apps add AI features, someone has to design how people use them, which is why AI interfaces are part of this roadmap.
